title: Redwood structured output & function-calling demo
summary: AE + SE walked through Redwood's structured output / JSON mode, schema enforcement, and function/tool-calling patterns. Customer was focused on reliable JSON outputs for downstream systems, auditability, and guardrails to prevent schema drift. SE demoed API calls and Console features (schema editor, failure modes, canned fallbacks). Next steps: send security docs, share benchmark checklist, get sample prompts/schemas and schedule a pilot run.
next_steps: Lena to send SOC2 + security pack and sample SAML config - due 2025-12-03
Marco to share benchmark checklist and dedicated capacity pricing - due 2025-12-05
Ben to upload 2 sample prompt sets and expected JSON schemas - due 2025-12-04
Schedule pilot benchmarking call for week of 2025-12-09
action_items: Lena Park - send SOC2 and security slide deck - 2025-12-03
Marco Diaz - share benchmark checklist, throughput test plan, and sample curl commands - 2025-12-05
Ben Miller - provide sample prompts, expected schema examples, and a small dataset for tests - 2025-12-04
header: Date: 2025-12-02 | Start: 14:30 PST | Duration: 48 min | Attendees: Redwood (Lena Park, Marco Diaz) + DataBridge (Aisha, Ben, Priya, Sam)
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm lena from Redwood Inference, with Marco our Solutions Eng. quick roll call?
[00:09] Aisha Khan: hi this is aisha, CTO at DataBridge. we got ben and priya and sam on as well.
[00:14] Marco Diaz: hi all, i'll be the demo voice today. quick agenda: show JSON mode/structured output, schema guardrails in the console, then function/tool calling patterns and how you can wire to downstream systems, and finally some optimize tips for cost/latency.
[00:29] Ben Miller: sounds good. our main ask is deterministic JSON output for ETL jobs, we want to avoid post-processing heuristics.
[00:36] Priya Rao: and audit logs + traceability. we need to show product that outputs stable fields to the analytics pipeline.
[00:42] Sam Ortiz: plus we run in a VPC, so we care about private deployment options and KMS encryption.
[00:48] Lena Park: totally. we'll cover hosted API and private options briefly and point you to the security pack. Marco, take it away.
[00:56] Marco Diaz: cool. opening the Console - apologies if names get mangled, the transcript sometimes says Rewood or Roodwood - uh minor transcript quirk. so first, JSON mode: you can pass a schema with required fields and types; the runtime enforces and if a model's raw output doesn't match the schema we can auto-apply a structured-extraction step and/or fallback to a stricter model variant.
[01:22] Marco Diaz: demo time. hitting the API in the corner here - curl example - content-type application/json, we set mode: "json_schema" and include the schema e.g. {"type": "object", "properties": {"customer_id": {"type": "string"}, "summary": {"type": "string"}, "entities": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "object", "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}, "score": {"type": "number"}}}}}} - the service returns a validated JSON blob.
[01:55] Ben Miller: if the model hallucinated an extra field, does it get stripped?
[02:00] Marco Diaz: good question. we have a couple options: strict mode will reject outputs that don't conform and return a structured error you can handle; permissive mode will drop unknown fields and attempt to coerce types. we also have an audit log of the raw tokens so you can trace where the value came from.
[02:18] Priya Rao: and how about tool calling - say we want Redwood to call an internal enrichment service with a parsed entity?
[02:25] Marco Diaz: two patterns: function-calling where the model returns a function name + arguments that Redwood converts into a call; or webhook/tool integrations where the platform posts the JSON to your endpoint in a secure VPC flow. here's a quick mock: model returns {"function": "enrich_customer", "args": {"customer_id": "123"}} then Redwood invokes that function or returns the payload to your orchestrator.
[02:47] Aisha Khan: are those tool calls recorded in the audit trail? we need end-to-end logs for compliance.
[02:53] Marco Diaz: yes, call-level logs, request/response bodies, and a trace id. in Private deployments logs can be forwarded to your SIEM; for hosted we support encrypted retention and role-based access.
[03:05] Ben Miller: latency - adding tool-calling step won't blow up 99th percentile right?
[03:10] Marco Diaz: generally you see an extra hop. we have async patterns: respond to client with structured partial result and run enrichment in background with webhook callback, or synchronous with fallback to cached data. for strict SLOs we recommend dedicated capacity.
[03:24] Lena Park: quick pause - on pricing and dedicated capacity we'll follow up with numbers; Marco will include throughput and expected token costs.
[03:31] Marco Diaz: moving on to guardrails - in the console you can create assertion rules: max array length, numeric bounds, regex patterns for strings. you can configure auto-retries with a different prompt template or fallback to a smaller hallucination-resistant model.
[03:48] Priya Rao: can we version schemas? our product wants to roll changes slowly.
[03:52] Marco Diaz: yes, schemas are versioned and you can pin deployments to schema versions; we also support canary rollouts and A/B tests for model variants.
[04:00] Ben Miller: and what about training data leakage concerns? we need to ensure customer PII never gets stored in model cache.
[04:06] Marco Diaz: we have opt-out and data retention controls; KV cache can be disabled or encrypted. for Private you can keep all logs on-prem. SOC2 details are in the pack Lena will share.
[04:17] Aisha Khan: good. show us a failure mode where model returns broken JSON and how Redwood handles it.
[04:23] Marco Diaz: demo: i run a prompt designed to elicit a complex nested object, intentionally nudge the model to produce malformed JSON - ok run shows raw token stream with missing brace. Redwood's extraction layer attempts to repair using a secondary parse pass and then validates; if it fails in strict mode you get an error object with diagnostics, including model variant, token snippet, and suggested prompt correction.
[04:49] Ben Miller: interesting. can we plug in our own sanitizer step before it hits the pipeline?
[04:54] Marco Diaz: yep, you can supply a pre-hook lambda or an API gateway function in private networks. many customers run a lightweight schema validator in their pipeline as a final gate.
[05:02] Sam Ortiz: VPC - how does the private agent connect? we use shared VPCs and strict egress policies.
[05:09] Marco Diaz: for Private we provide an appliance or container bundle that you run in your network; it calls home only on the control plane channel secured by mutual TLS. we can also do air-gapped installs with a compliance engagement.
[05:22] Lena Park: question from my side - what scale are you expecting for the pilot? tokens per second or per month?
[05:27] Ben Miller: prototype starts small ~10k tokens/day then jump to 1-2M/day if things go well.
[05:33] Marco Diaz: that maps well to a pilot on hosted then dedicated if throughput increases. we'll include batching suggestions - for short-turn prompts batching reduces per-token overhead but watch tail latency.
[05:45] Marco Diaz: demoing function calling now: create function schema in the Console - we define name, input schema, auth header template. then the model is prompted to return the function call. watch this: sending a chat request with system instruction: "Use function 'fetch_customer' to return structured customer object when possible" - model returns function call, Redwood validates args and posts to the configured URL.
[06:07] Priya Rao: how do we handle secrets for the function call? we don't want tokens in logs.
[06:12] Marco Diaz: we inject secrets server-side using KMS; secrets are never exposed in raw event bodies in logs unless you opt-in. in private, you can bring your own KMS/HSM.
[06:22] Aisha Khan: can the function call be reversible - like if enrichment fails, do we rollback or mark as failed?
[06:28] Marco Diaz: the platform emits a structured event with status; you can configure retries, dead-letter queues, and a compensating transaction hook. we don't do DB rollbacks automatically, that lives in your orchestrator.
[06:40] Lena Park: quick aside: some customers use a hybrid where Redwood returns both the parsed JSON and the raw text under a "_raw" key for traces. helps with debugging.
[06:50] Ben Miller: yep would be useful.
[06:53] Marco Diaz: moving to Optimize recommendations: we analyze token patterns and recommend quantization, per-route batching, and prefix caching. for stable structured outputs we recommend smaller context windows and pinned model versions to avoid drift.
[07:08] Ben Miller: any benchmarks you can share for JSON-mode reliability? like percent of valid schema returns?
[07:13] Marco Diaz: we have internal benchmarks: on curated evaluation sets strict-mode validation success ~92% on top-tier models, with extraction/repair pushing effective success >98%. i'll share the benchmark csv.
[07:25] Priya Rao: we need to see those evals end-to-end with our prompts.
[07:29] Marco Diaz: absolutely - next step: you send prompts and expected schema, we'll run a pilot and return a report.
[07:35] Aisha Khan: security doc timeline?
[07:37] Lena Park: i'll send earlier tomorrow, SOC2 and network diagrams.
[07:40] Sam Ortiz: one more nit: we use SAML SSO and RBAC for audits.
[07:45] Marco Diaz: supported - we have SAML, SCIM, RBAC mappings, and per-route API keys.
[07:52] Ben Miller: ok demo complete. can you show a short CLI example for invoking JSON mode with function calling?
[07:56] Marco Diaz: sure - curl POST to /v1/chat with body: {"model": "rwd-llm-1", "mode": "json_schema", "schema": <schema>, "functions": [<fn defs>], "messages": [...] } response: {"status": "ok", "output": {"customer_id": "123", "summary": "..."}, "function_calls": [{"name": "enrich_customer", "args": {"customer_id": "123"}}], "trace_id": "trace-xyz" }
[08:29] Lena Park: circling back to procurement: typical pilot flow is free credits for a limited run, then usage-based for hosted or a committed monthly for dedicated. we can loop in sales for contract terms.
[08:40] Aisha Khan: good. any blockers you foresee?
[08:43] Marco Diaz: only major one is if you need air-gapped deployment quickly; that adds timeline. otherwise it's mostly integration and prompt/schema engineering.
[08:52] Priya Rao: thanks - this was helpful. we'll compile a short success criteria doc: 1) 95% schema validity on our prompts, 2) end-to-end latency < 500ms p50 for real-time UI, 3) full audit trail to our SIEM.
[09:08] Lena Park: perfect - we'll work to meet that in the pilot.
[09:12] Marco Diaz: last q: any specific downstream systems we should know?
[09:15] Ben Miller: we pipe JSON into Snowflake via a Kafka topic, so keys and types must be stable.
[09:21] Marco Diaz: noted - we'll make sure sample outputs are Snowflake-friendly and avoid nested type surprises.
[09:28] Lena Park: wrap up - thanks all. action items and next steps we'll follow up in an email.
[09:33] Aisha Khan: thanks lena, marco. bye.
[09:35] End of recording (approx).
